85	### 2.5 Who did it: identity in CloudTrail
86	
87	| # | Finding | Marker | Source |
88	|---|---|---|---|
89	| 2.5.1 | For Identity Center's own events (sign-in, portal, CLI login), the user is identified by `userId` and `identityStoreArn` in `userIdentity.onBehalfOf`. The `userIdentity` type is `IdentityCenterUser` or `Unknown`, and workflows "should accept both". "The `userName` and `principalId` fields under the `userIdentity` element are no longer available." The docs give two ways to get the username: look it up in the directory (`identitystore describe-user`), or read the `UserName` that Identity Center emits under `additionalEventData` in sign-in events. | ✅ | [IC sso-cloudtrail-use-cases](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/sso-cloudtrail-use-cases.html), [CT cloudtrail-event-reference-user-identity](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-event-reference-user-identity.html) |
90	| 2.5.2 | The portal API events include `ListAccounts`, `ListAccountRoles`, `GetRoleCredentials` and `Logout`; "Using the AWS CLI can lead to the emission of CloudTrail events" from both public and non-public portal operations. | ✅ | [IC sso-info-in-cloudtrail](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/sso-info-in-cloudtrail.html) |
91	| 2.5.3 | **Partly resolved, by inference from docs:** how a call made *with a permission-set role* in a member account (for example `ecs:UpdateService` in prod) names the human in CloudTrail. The chain of evidence:
92	- For SAML-federated and assumed-role principals, `aws:userid` is `role-id:caller-specified-role-name`.
93	- CloudTrail's `principalId` for temporary credentials "includes the session name".
94	- For Identity Center users, `aws:userId` "can change if the user's username or email address changes".
95	- Together: the role session name is derived from the Identity Center username or email, and it appears in `userIdentity.principalId` / `arn`.
96	
97	Two consequences:
98	- It is **not a stable audit key**, because it changes when the username changes.
99	- Whether `onBehalfOf.userId` also appears on these member-account events is **not stated** anywhere (test on a sandbox account).
100	
101	The TEAM blog (2.4.1b) says CloudTrail events carry "the unique identifier of the user". | ✅ (each quote) / ⚠️ (the combined inference; `onBehalfOf` in member accounts) | [IAM reference_policies_variables](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_variables.html), [CT user identity](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-event-reference-user-identity.html), [IC prereqs-revoking-user-permissions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/prereqs-revoking-user-permissions.html) |
102	| 2.5.4 | **Source identity:** an administrator can require roles to be assumed with a `sourceIdentity`. It "cannot be changed during the role session", it persists through role chaining, and it is logged in `sessionContext`. Caveats: "AWS doesn't control the value of the source identity". The docs say "you must choose an attribute that you want your users or IdP to provide" and "you must ensure that you can control how those values are provided". **Asserted by the IdP**, the value is trustworthy; **supplied by the caller**, it is only a hint. Setting it needs `sts:SetSourceIdentity` in the role trust policy. It is "not captured by CloudTrail when an AWS service or service-linked role carries out an action on behalf of" a workforce identity. The pages read do not say whether permission-set roles, whose trust policy Identity Center manages, can require it. | ✅ / ⚠️ (permission sets) | [IAM id_credentials_temp_control-access_monitor](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_temp_control-access_monitor.html), [CT user identity](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-event-reference-user-identity.html) |
103	| 2.5.5 | **AWS MCP Server in CloudTrail:**
104	- "All AWS MCP Server actions for authenticated tools are logged by CloudTrail". An example is the `CallReadWriteTool` action, whose event includes an "Exact copy of MCP request params".
105	- With OAuth, Sign-In also logs `AuthorizeOAuth2Access` and `CreateOAuth2Token`, including the OAuth client ID and the sign-in session ARN. API calls made with OAuth tokens carry `aws:SignInSessionArn` "to correlate API activity with the originating OAuth sign-in session".
106	- **PHI note (inference):** the copied request params can contain query text or data (1.11).
107	
108	| ✅ / ⚠️ (PHI note) | [Agent Toolkit: logging-using-cloudtrail](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/logging-using-cloudtrail.html), [IAM condition keys: aws:SignInSessionArn](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_condition-keys.html#condition-keys-signinsessionarn) |
109	
110	### 2.6 CloudTrail as the audit store
111	
112	| # | Finding | Marker | Source |
113	|---|---|---|---|
114	| 2.6.1 | **Event history** is on by default: "the past 90 days of **management** events in an AWS Region". It shows no data events. A trail or an event data store is needed for an ongoing record. | ✅ | [CT view-cloudtrail-events](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/view-cloudtrail-events.html) |
115	| 2.6.2 | An **organization trail**, created from the management account or a CloudTrail delegated administrator, logs the management account and all member accounts. Member-account users "do not have sufficient permissions to delete organization trails, turn logging on or off, change what types of events are logged". New accounts are added automatically. | ✅ | [CT creating-trail-organization](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/creating-trail-organization.html) |
116	| 2.6.3 | **Data events are off by default** and cost extra ("By default, trails and event data stores do not log data events. Additional charges apply"). Advanced event selectors can filter by resource and `eventName`. Resource types relevant to Papaya include `AWS::S3::Object`, `AWS::Lambda::Function` (Invoke), `AWS::SQS::Queue`, `AWS::SNS::Topic`, `AWS::StepFunctions::StateMachine`, `AWS::SSM::ManagedNode`, and `AWS::RDS::DBCluster`. The last one covers **RDS Data API only**. | ✅ | [CT logging-data-events-with-cloudtrail](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/logging-data-events-with-cloudtrail.html) |
117	| 2.6.4 | **Log file integrity validation:** SHA-256 hashes plus hourly digest files signed with SHA-256 with RSA, which make it "computationally infeasible to modify, delete or forge CloudTrail log files without detection". Validation can also "assert positively that no log files were delivered … during a given period". | ✅ | [CT cloudtrail-log-file-validation-intro](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-log-file-validation-intro.html) |
118	| 2.6.5 | Preventive best practices: a **separate log archive account** with a dedicated S3 bucket, SSE-KMS, least-privilege bucket policy with `aws:SourceArn`, and MFA delete on the log bucket. MFA delete cannot be combined with lifecycle configurations. **Retention:** "The CloudTrail trail default is to store log files indefinitely" in the bucket; lifecycle rules are how to expire them. So a retention period and MFA delete need a deliberate choice. | ✅ | [CT best-practices-security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/best-practices-security.html) |
119	| 2.6.6 | **CloudTrail Lake "will no longer be open to new customers starting May 31, 2026."** Existing customers continue. As of the access date (2026-11-08), a design must not assume Papaya can adopt it, unless Papaya already uses it (⚠️ unknown). | ✅ | [CT cloudtrail-lake](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-lake.html) |
120	
121	### 2.7 Audit gaps below the AWS API: Aurora
122	
123	| # | Finding | Marker | Source |
124	|---|---|---|---|
125	| 2.7.1 | SQL sent over a normal PostgreSQL connection is **not** an AWS API call. CloudTrail data events for RDS cover only the Data API (2.6.3). So `SELECT`/`UPDATE` run by a person or an agent through `psql` leaves no CloudTrail record. | ✅ (Data API scope) / ⚠️ inference (no page states the negative) | [CT data events](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/logging-data-events-with-cloudtrail.html) |
126	| 2.7.2 | **Database Activity Streams (Aurora PostgreSQL):** a near-real-time activity stream pushed to Kinesis, always encrypted with KMS. Separation from DBAs needs configuration: "you can control administrator access to data streams by configuring the Database Activity Streams feature. DBAs don't have access to the collection, transmission, storage, and processing of the streams".
127	- **Asynchronous mode:** records "might have been lost" during errors.
128	- **Synchronous mode:** the session waits until the record is durable, but "if the event can't be made durable for some reason, the database session returns to normal activities", and an RDS event says records might be lost.
129	- **Both modes:** loss is signalled by RDS events, which need an alert.
130	
131	The rest of this row: It must be stopped before a major version upgrade. Supported PostgreSQL instance classes are listed (r4–r8g, r6id, x2g); **db.serverless is not listed** (⚠️: confirm Serverless v2 support if Papaya uses it). Kinesis is charged. | ✅ / ⚠️ (Serverless v2) | [Aurora DBActivityStreams](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/DBActivityStreams.html) |
132	| 2.7.3 | **Inference:** an activity stream records SQL statements, and literals in them can carry PHI (1.11). The audit stream is then itself a PHI-bearing store (add to 1.11.4 L15). `pgaudit` is the in-engine alternative; **not researched this session** (⚠️). | ⚠️ inference | — |

135	
136	| # | Finding | Marker | Source |
137	|---|---|---|---|
138	| 2.8.1 | Custom policy checks: `check-no-new-access` (does the new version grant more than the old?), `check-access-not-granted` (does it grant listed actions?), `check-no-public-access`. Each check is charged. | ✅ | [IAM access-analyzer-custom-policy-checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-custom-policy-checks.html) |
139	
140	### 2.9 What this means for Papaya (inferences — to be used in the design)
141	
142	These are my conclusions from the findings above, not documented facts:
143	
144	1. **On a laptop, an agent that calls the AWS CLI/SDK directly is indistinguishable from the
145	   engineer.**
146	   - **Why:** it uses the same SSO cache, and that cache reaches every role assigned to the
147	     engineer (2.2.1, 2.2.2). App ID is a client hint (2.2.3). Source identity is trustworthy only
148	     when the IdP asserts it (2.5.4).
149	   - **Consequence:** a separate "agent" permission set alone does not separate the two. The
150	     agent can still use the engineer's other roles from the same cache.
151	   - **The one native, server-set signal is the AWS MCP Server** (2.2.4, 2.2.5). Calls through it
152	     carry `aws:ViaAWSMCPService` / `aws:CalledViaAWSMCP`, usable in SCPs. They are absent on
153	     direct calls, so the signal works as a control only if direct calls are blocked for the
154	     agent. One way: an agent-only role whose policy denies any request where
155	     `aws:ViaAWSMCPService` is not `true` (⚠️ design idea; test it, including `aws___run_script`).
156	   - **The decisive layer remains no standing prod-write assignment for humans** (#2). Then
157	     nothing running on the laptop can write to prod outside an approved, time-boxed window.
158	     **Inside that window,** any process on the laptop can use the grant. This is a residual risk
159	     to state openly.
160	2. **Changing prod: the default path is a pipeline; human write access is the exception, via JIT.**
161	   - **Default path:** humans hold no prod-write rights. Changes go through CI with a deploy role.
162	     The named-human approval happens at the CI gate (GitHub Environments, Topic 3).
163	   - **JIT, for the rest:** when a human needs write access (manual operations, incidents), it
164	     comes from a JIT assignment. AWS has no native request/approve feature (2.4.1). The options:
165	     - a partner product (2.4.1);
166	     - the TEAM sample (2.4.1b);
167	     - a small home-built flow on `CreateAccountAssignment` / `DeleteAccountAssignment` (2.4.2).
168	   - **Audit evidence:** CloudTrail records the **grant**, and its caller is the automation role.
169	     It does **not** record the approver. The approver's identity lives in the approval system
170	     (GitHub, Linear, the partner tool, TEAM). It must be linked to the grant, for example by
171	     request ID, and kept as audit evidence (⚠️ design).
172	   - **Incidents:** under GĐ-8 the incident path is the same flow with a fast approver, not a
173	     bypass.
174	   - **Outage path:** the emergency direct-federation path (2.1.11) is for an Identity Center
175	     outage, and needs its own approval and alerting.
176	3. **Revocation is slow by design.**
177	   - Role sessions outlive portal sessions and assignments (2.4.3). IAM's revoke button does not
178	     apply to permission-set roles (2.4.6).
179	   - Prod permission sets should use the **1-hour minimum** session duration (2.1.4).
180	   - Pre-deploy the `identitystore:userId` Deny SCP on the prod OU (2.4.4), and keep the
181	     `aws:TokenIssueTime` Deny as an org-wide kill switch (2.4.6).
182	   - Set the portal session length deliberately (2.1.5, 2.1.6), including the IdP session,
183	     which can silently extend it.
184	4. **SCPs are the guardrail the agent cannot edit, but only in member accounts.** Examples:
185	   - protect the org trail and the log archive (2.6.2);
186	   - deny region drift;
187	   - deny data-plane reads on PHI buckets and queues, except for the application roles **and**
188	     the approved JIT read path that GĐ-9 allows (`aws:PrincipalArn`; tenant scoping via ABAC
189	     session tags, 2.1.8). This supports 1.11.4 L3–L4;
190	   - deny destructive actions when `aws:ViaAWSMCPService` is true (2.2.5).
191	
192	   Constraints:
193	   - Keep everything out of the management account (2.3.2, 2.3.7).
194	   - Deny-list SCPs sit on `FullAWSAccess` (2.3.4b).
195	   - Limits are 10 direct attachments per target and 10,240 characters each (2.3.4).
196	   - RCPs add an outside-the-org boundary for S3, SQS, KMS, Secrets Manager and Logs, but not for
197	     Aurora, Lambda or SNS (2.3.6).
198	5. **Audit trail for Compliance:**
199	   - **Trail:** an organization trail to a separate log-archive account, with integrity validation
200	     and a locked-down bucket (2.6.2, 2.6.4, 2.6.5).
201	   - **Retention:** decide it explicitly. The default is indefinite, and MFA delete excludes
202	     lifecycle rules (2.6.5).
203	   - **Data events:** only where they matter, because of cost (2.6.3): PHI buckets, prod Lambda
204	     invoke, prod SQS.
205	   - **No CloudTrail Lake** (2.6.6).
206	   - **Who did it:** use `identitystore:UserId` / `onBehalfOf.userId` where present. The session
207	     name changes when the username changes, so it is not a stable key (2.5.3).
208	   - **Aurora:** SQL is invisible to CloudTrail (2.7.1). Use Database Activity Streams or pgaudit,
209	     alert on the RDS events about lost records, and treat that stream as PHI (2.7.2, 2.7.3).
210	   - **Same gap for shell sessions:** ECS Exec and SSM shell sessions likely have the same issue
211	     (⚠️ not researched, 2.10).
212	6. **Policy changes in Pulumi PRs can be checked mechanically.** `check-no-new-access` in CI makes
213	   "this PR widens IAM" a visible, reviewable fact (2.8.1; ties to Topics 3–4).
214	
215	### 2.10 Open items (Topic 2)
216	
217	- [ ] ⚠️ Does `onBehalfOf.userId` appear on member-account events made with a permission-set role,
218	      and what exactly is the session name (2.5.3)? Test on a sandbox account.
219	- [ ] ⚠️ Do profiles sharing one `sso-session` reuse the single cached token (2.2.2)? Test.
220	- [ ] ⚠️ Agent-only role that denies non-MCP calls (`aws:ViaAWSMCPService`), including how
221	      `aws___run_script` calls are seen (2.2.5, 2.9 #1). Test.
222	- [ ] ⚠️ Can permission-set roles (or account-access-manager roles) require `sts:SetSourceIdentity`
223	      (2.5.4, 2.1.10)?
224	- [ ] ⚠️ Does Papaya use an external IdP (MFA and session length then live there, 2.1.5, 2.1.7),
225	      Aurora Serverless v2 (2.7.2), or CloudTrail Lake already (2.6.6)?
226	- [ ] ⚠️ Not researched: `pgaudit` on Aurora PostgreSQL; Athena over CloudTrail in S3; ECS Exec and
227	      SSM Session Manager logging of commands; S3 Object Lock for the CloudTrail bucket; whether
228	      App ID shows in CloudTrail `userAgent`.
229	
230	### 2.11 Review log (Topic 2)
231	
232	- **Round 1 (2026-11-08)**, independent reviewer subagent. Sources: the raw AWS pages, plus
233	  pages it fetched itself (IAM policy variables, the TEAM blog).

236	    keys and the Agent Toolkit pages, SCP evaluation, IAM revoke page, retention sentence, CLI

241	    - 2.9 #2 reframed: the pipeline is the default path, JIT is for human access;
242	    - 2.2.2 backed by docs;
243	    - 2.5.3 partly resolved;
244	    - 2.9 #1 rewritten with the MCP keys and the limits of a separate agent role;
245	    - 2.7.2 qualifiers.

247	    (2.4.1b), IAM revoke and `aws:TokenIssueTime` (2.4.6), and CloudTrail retention (2.6.5).

12:+ **Option A: OAuth (simple)** — Connect to AWS MCP Server using OAuth. If you are a human user, you authenticate in your browser. If you are running an automated agent, it authenticates by requesting a token. Works for web clients (such as Claude.ai and ChatGPT.com) and most IDE, terminal, or desktop-based clients. Use this option if you are new to AWS and use a single account, or if you int
13:+ **Option B: SigV4 (advanced)** — Authenticate using the AWS CLI, then use the MCP Proxy for AWS to sign requests with SigV4 credentials. Use this option if you use terminal or IDE-based coding agents (such as Claude Code, Kiro, and Codex), or if you need to switch between AWS accounts frequently.
25:| Do you want to get started without installing uvx, installing the AWS CLI, or configuring local credentials? | OAuth | 
26:| Does your client only support remote MCP servers (no local process)? | OAuth | 
27:| Does your agent need access across multiple AWS accounts in the same session? | SigV4 | 
28:| Do you need read-only mode (hide write-capable tools from the agent entirely)? | SigV4 | 
29:| Does your organization restrict the signin:AuthorizeOAuth2Access and signin:CreateOAuth2Token permissions needed for browser-based OAuth login? | SigV4 | 
30:| Do you need to set a default AWS Region for your agentic session (without specifying it in every query)? | SigV4 | 
31:| Does your client not support the OAuth flow but can run a local MCP proxy? | SigV4 | 
42:If you are currently using the AWS API MCP Server or AWS Knowledge MCP Server, we recommend switching to the AWS MCP Server. The AWS MCP Server is a managed remote MCP server that reduces setup and maintenance effort and offers enhanced security controls through IAM condition keys.

53:   + `aws-knowledge-mcp-server`

125:Add as a remote MCP server with URL: `https://aws-mcp.us-east-1.api.aws/mcp?oauth=initialize`

174:If your client is not listed above, use the default endpoint URL (`https://aws-mcp.us-east-1.api.aws/mcp`). If tool calls fail due to credential errors, append `?oauth=initialize` to the URL to instruct the server to explicitly trigger the OAuth flow.

content.content: 18:+ `aws___run_script` - Execute Python code in a sandboxed environment with AWS API access. Use for tasks that involve listing resources and checking their properties, parallel API calls, multi-step workflows, cross-service checks, and retry logic. 20:+ `aws___get_tasks` - Poll the status of long-running tasks started by `aws___run_script`. Use when a previous tool call returns a task ID with a working status. 24:When multiple profiles are configured (via `--profile` or `AWS_MCP_PROXY_PROFILES`), the MCP Proxy for AWS injects an optional `aws_profile` parameter into the schema of `aws___run_script`, `aws___get_presigned_url`, and `aws___get_tasks`. This parameter lets the agent route individual requests through different AWS credential profiles. The parameter is stripped by the proxy before forwarding to the server. See [Multi-profile support](multi-account-access.md) for configuration details. ---- # How AWS MCP Server works with IAM AWS MCP Server uses a simplified authorization model that works like the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and AWS SDKs. The server does not define its own IAM actions, resources, or service-specific condition keys. Instead, it authenticates your request using [SigV4](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_sigv.html), adds standardized condition context keys, and forwards the request to the downstream AWS service. The downstream service performs the authorization check using your existing IAM policies. This means your AI agents work with your existing AWS credentials and service-level permissions, and you do not need to configure separate MCP-specific IAM actions. ## Authorization flow When an AI agent calls the AWS MCP Server, the following authorization flow occurs: 1. Your agent's request is authenticated with your AWS credentials using [SigV4](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_sigv.html). The [MCP Proxy for AWS](https://github.com/aws/mcp-proxy-for-aws) handles this signing automatically between your host application and the server. 1. AWS MCP Server authenticates the request and adds the MCP condition context keys (`aws:ViaAWSMCPService` and `aws:CalledViaAWSMCP`). 1. AWS MCP Server forwards the request to the target AWS service. 1. The target AWS service authorizes the request using your existing IAM policies, which can reference the MCP condition context keys for fine-grained control. ## MCP condition context keys AWS MCP Server automatically adds the following global condition context keys to all requests it forwards to downstream AWS services. You can use these keys in IAM policies and service control policies (SCPs) to differentiate between requests made through an AWS managed MCP server and direct API calls. `aws:ViaAWSMCPService` A Boolean key set to `true` for any request that passes through an AWS managed MCP server. Use this key to allow or deny all actions initiated through any AWS managed MCP server. Type: Boolean `aws:CalledViaAWSMCP` A single-valued string key containing the service principal of the specific AWS managed MCP server that initiated the request. Use this key to apply controls for a specific MCP server. Type: String Example values: + `aws-mcp.amazonaws.com` – AWS MCP Server + `eks-mcp.amazonaws.com` – Amazon EKS MCP Server + `ecs-mcp.amazonaws.com` – Amazon ECS MCP Server For more information about global condition context keys, see [IAM condition context keys](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_condition-keys.html) in the *IAM User Guide*. ## OAuth condition keys for AWS Sign-in When you use OAuth authentication with AWS MCP Server through AWS Sign-in, the following service-specific condition keys are available in the `signin:` namespace. Use these keys in IAM policies and SCPs to govern how OAuth is used within your organization. `signin:OAuthClientId` The ARN of the OAuth client making the request. Use this key to allow only approved OAuth clients to access AWS MCP Server. Type: String (ARN) Applies to: `signin:AuthorizeOAuth2Access`, `signin:CreateOAuth2Token` `signin:OAuthRedirectUri` The redirect URI used in the authorization request. Use this key to restrict token delivery to trusted redirect URIs such as localhost or corporate domains. Type: String Applies to: `signin:AuthorizeOAuth2Access` `signin:OAuthGrantType` The OAuth grant type being used. Use this key to control which OAuth authorization flows are permitted. Type: String Example values: `authorization_code`, `refresh_token`, `client_credentials` Applies to: `signin:CreateOAuth2Token` `signin:OAuthClientAuthentication` The client authentication method used. Use this key to require specific authentication methods. Type: String Example values: `none`, `client_secret_basic`, `client_secret_post` Applies to: `signin:CreateOAuth2Token` OAuth access tokens carry the `aws:SignInSessionArn` global condition key. This key contains the unique ARN of the AWS Sign-in session. For more information about OAuth condition keys, see [OAuth condition keys reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/signin/latest/userguide/reference-signin-condition-keys.html) in the *AWS Sign-in User Guide*. For OAuth authentication setup and governance examples, see [OAuth 2.1 authentication for AWS MCP Server](oauth-authentication.md). ## Identity-based policies **Supports identity-based policies:** Yes Because AWS MCP Server forwards requests to downstream AWS services using your credentials, the IAM policies attached to your IAM user or role determine what actions the MCP server can perform on your behalf. No additional IAM configuration is required to use AWS MCP Server beyond the permissions you already grant for direct API access. You can use the MCP condition context keys in your existing policies to apply different permissions when actions are initiated through an MCP server. For examples, see [Identity-based policy examples for AWS MCP Server](security_iam_id-based-policy-examples.md). ## Using temporary credentials with AWS MCP Server

When you authenticate with AWS MCP Server, you can use temporary credentials from IAM roles, federated identities, or assumed roles. The server forwards these credentials to downstream AWS services, which honor the same session policies and permission boundaries as direct API calls. ## Deprecated MCP-specific IAM actions During the preview period, AWS MCP Server required the following service-specific IAM actions: + `aws-mcp:InvokeMcp` + `aws-mcp:CallReadOnlyTool` + `aws-mcp:CallReadWriteTool` These actions are no longer required and have no effect. content.content: # Logging AWS MCP Server API calls using AWS CloudTrail AWS MCP Server is integrated with AWS CloudTrail, a service that provides a record of actions taken by a user, role, or an AWS service in AWS MCP Server. CloudTrail captures all API calls for AWS MCP Server as events. The calls captured include calls from the AWS MCP Server console and code calls to the AWS MCP Server API operations. If you create a trail, you can enable continuous delivery of CloudTrail events to an Amazon S3 bucket, including events for AWS MCP Server. If you don't configure a trail, you can still view the most recent events in the CloudTrail console in **Event history**. Using the information collected by CloudTrail, you can determine the request that was made to AWS MCP To learn more about CloudTrail, see the [AWS CloudTrail User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-user-guide.html). ## AWS MCP Server information in CloudTrail CloudTrail is enabled on your AWS account when you create the account. When activity occurs in AWS MCP Server, that activity is recorded in a CloudTrail event along with other AWS service events in **Event history**. You can view, search, and download recent events in your AWS account. For more information, see [Viewing events with CloudTrail Event history](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/view-cloudtrail-events.html). For an ongoing record of events in your AWS account, including events for AWS MCP Server, create a trail. A *trail* enables CloudTrail to deliver log files to an Amazon S3 bucket. By default, when you create a trail in the console, the trail applies to all AWS Regions. The trail logs events from all Regions in the AWS partition and delivers the log files to the Amazon S3 bucket that you specify. Additionally, you can configure other AWS services to further analyze and act upon the event data collected in CloudTrail logs. For more information, see the following: + [Overview for creating a trail](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-create-and-update-a-trail.html) + [CloudTrail supported services and integrations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-aws-service-specific-topics.html) + [Configuring Amazon SNS notifications for CloudTrail](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/configure-sns-notifications-for-cloudtrail.html) + [Receiving CloudTrail log files from multiple regions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/receive-cloudtrail-log-files-from-multiple-regions.html) and [Receiving CloudTrail log files from multiple accounts](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-receive-logs-from-multiple-accounts.html) All AWS MCP Server actions for authenticated tools are logged by CloudTrail and are documented in the [Agent Toolkit for AWS API Reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-mcp/latest/APIReference/). For example, calls to the `CallReadWriteTool` action generate entries in the CloudTrail log files. When you use OAuth authentication, CloudTrail also records the following AWS Sign-in events: + `AuthorizeOAuth2Access` — Recorded when a user authorizes an OAuth flow for an MCP client. + `CreateOAuth2Token` — Recorded when AWS Sign-in issues or refreshes OAuth tokens. These events include the OAuth client ID, target AWS MCP Server resource, redirect URI, and associated sign-in session ARN. API calls made using OAuth access tokens include the `aws:SignInSessionArn` context. Use this context to correlate API activity with the originating OAuth sign-in session. For examples of CloudTrail entries for OAuth events, see [Monitoring OAuth activity](oauth-authentication.md#oauth-monitoring). Every event or log entry contains information about who generated the request. The identity information helps you determine the following: + Whether the request was made with root or AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) user credentials. + Whether the request was made with temporary security credentials for a role or federated user. + Whether the request was made by another AWS service. For more information, see the [CloudTrail userIdentity element](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-event-reference-user-identity.html). ## Understanding AWS MCP Server log file entries A trail is a configuration that enables delivery of events as log files to an Amazon S3 bucket that you specify. CloudTrail log files contain one or more log entries. An event represents a single request from any source and includes information about the requested action, the date and time of the action, request parameters, and so on. CloudTrail log files aren't an ordered stack trace of the public API calls, so they don't appear in any specific order. **Important** Tool names in CloudTrail logs may not match exactly the tools shown in your MCP client. For example: MCP client shows: `aws___retrieve_skill` CloudTrail logs show: `retrieve_skill` This occurs because CloudTrail logs the tool name without the namespace prefix used by MCP clients. The following example shows a CloudTrail log entry that demonstrates the `CallReadWriteTool` action. ``` { "eventVersion": "1.08", "eventCategory": "Data", "eventType": "AwsMcpEvent", "userIdentity": { ... }, "eventTime": "...", "eventSource": "aws-mcp.amazonaws.com", "eventName": "CallReadWriteTool", "awsRegion": "us-east-1", "sourceIPAddress": "...", "delegatedViaAWS": "...", "requestParameters": { "method": "tools/call", "params": { // Exact copy of MCP request params }, "id": "request-id" }, "responseElements": { "content": [ { "type": "text", "text": "example" } ], "isError": false }, "requestID": "12345678-1234-1234-1234-123456789012", "eventID": "87654321-4321-4321-4321-210987654321", "readOnly": true, "recipientAccountId": "123456789012", "resources": [ { "type": "AWS::S3::Bucket", "ARN": "arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket-1", "accountId": "123456789012" } ], "mcpEventDetails": { } } ] ``` ## Restrict actions to a specific MCP server The following policy denies all actions when the request comes specifically through AWS MCP Server, while allowing requests from other AWS managed MCP servers or direct API calls. ``` { "Sid": "DenyActionsViaAWSMCPServer", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:CalledViaAWSMCP": "aws-mcp.amazonaws.com" } } } ```

# Identity-based policy examples for AWS MCP Server The following examples show how to use IAM policies with the MCP condition context keys to control access through AWS MCP Server. Each example shows the policy statement to include within your IAM policy document. **Topics** + [Deny all actions through any AWS managed MCP server](#security_iam_id-based-policy-examples-deny-all-mcp) + [Deny destructive actions through AWS MCP Server](#security_iam_id-based-policy-examples-deny-destructive) + [Restrict actions to a specific MCP server](#security_iam_id-based-policy-examples-restrict-specific-server) ## Deny all actions through any AWS managed MCP server The following SCP or IAM policy denies all actions when the request originates from any AWS managed MCP server. Nguồn đã đối chiếu: scratchpad/docs/aws/ và scratchpad/docs/aws-mcp/ (getting-started, service-with-iam, id-based-policy-examples, logging-using-cloudtrail, understanding-mcp-server-tools). Không có ID thật nào: `123456789012` và `us-east-1` chỉ nằm trong ví dụ của nguồn, không có trong ghi chú.

## Trạng thái các finding vòng 1

| ID | Trạng thái | Ghi chú |
|---|---|---|
| F1 | FIXED | 2.9 #2 nay nói rõ CloudTrail ghi grant, không ghi người duyệt |
| F2 | FIXED | Pipeline là đường mặc định, JIT là ngoại lệ |
| F3 | FIXED | 2.2.2 có trích dẫn từ docs; phần reuse token vẫn ⚠️ |
| F4 | FIXED | 2.5.3: chuỗi suy luận có nhãn ⚠️; `onBehalfOf` để test |

## Lỗi mới

**N1, MEDIUM, 2.9 #1: ý tưởng "agent-only role denies non-MCP calls".**
- Đã có nhãn "⚠️ design idea; test it". Nhưng câu "One way" vẫn nói quá, và lập luận mâu thuẫn với chính dòng trước nó.
- Role này chỉ ràng buộc chính nó. Chính 2.9 #1 và 2.2.2 nói agent vẫn gọi trực tiếp CLI được bằng các role của engineer qua cùng cache. Vậy role này không làm "direct calls are blocked for the agent".
- Với SigV4 (2.2.4), proxy cục bộ đọc credential của AWS CLI trên laptop, chạy dưới cùng OS user. Agent buộc phải đọc được nơi chứa credential, trừ khi proxy chạy ngoài sandbox của agent. Docs viết: "Authenticate using the AWS CLI, then use the MCP Proxy for AWS to sign requests". Proxy còn có tham số `aws_profile` để định tuyến qua nhiều profile (understanding-mcp-server-tools).
- OAuth thì không dùng credential cục bộ. Docs có ghi "Claude Code CLI" trong nhóm hỗ trợ OAuth đầy đủ, nhưng "Multi-profile switching… is not supported with OAuth".
- Docs chỉ có ví dụ *deny khi đi qua MCP*. Không có ví dụ *chỉ cho phép qua MCP*. Ý tưởng này là thiết kế không có trong tài liệu.
- Sửa:
  - Ghi rõ điều kiện cần là agent không tới được credential của engineer, nhờ sandbox ở Topic 1.6 hoặc OAuth thay cho SigV4. Thiếu điều kiện đó, role riêng không tạo ra kiểm soát nào.
  - Ghi rõ đây là ý tưởng không có trong docs.
  - Thêm vào 2.10 hai việc cần test: chọn toán tử điều kiện (xem N5); `aws___get_presigned_url`, vì việc tải S3 bằng presigned URL do client làm trực tiếp, có thể không mang key MCP (⚠️).

**N2, MEDIUM, 2.5.5: "All AWS MCP Server actions … are logged by CloudTrail".**
- Event mẫu trên chính trang đó có `"eventCategory": "Data"`, `"eventType": "AwsMcpEvent"`.
- Theo 2.6.3, data event mặc định bị tắt. Bảng data-event của CloudTrail (bản tải hôm nay) không có resource type nào cho `aws-mcp`; chỉ có `AWS::AgentAccessMCP::Tools` của WorkSpaces.
- Trang MCP cũng nói xem được trong Event history, mà Event history chỉ hiện management event. Docs mâu thuẫn hoặc chưa đủ.
- Sửa: đánh ⚠️ cho câu "logged by default by a normal trail". Thêm open item: cần event selector nào. 2.9 #5 không được giả định đã có các event này.

**N3, MEDIUM, 2.5.5, ghi chú PHI.**
- Event mẫu có `responseElements.content[].text`, tức là đầu ra của tool. Không chỉ có "Exact copy of MCP request params".
- Vậy *kết quả* do agent đọc được (có thể là dữ liệu PHI) cũng có thể nằm trong CloudTrail.

| 2.2.4 | **AWS MCP Server** (Agent Toolkit for AWS) is "a managed remote MCP server". AWS recommends it over the older local `aws-api-mcp-server` / `aws-knowledge-mcp-server`. There are two auth options: **OAuth** (browser sign-in via AWS Sign-In), and **SigV4** through the local "MCP Proxy for AWS" using AWS CLI credentials. The docs recommend SigV4 ("Use this option if you use terminal or IDE-based coding agents (such as Claude Code, Kiro, and Codex)"), but they also list "Claude Code CLI" as an OAuth client. "Multi-profile switching for cross-account workflows is not supported with OAuth." Read-only mode ("hide write-capable tools from the agent entirely") is available with SigV4. **Inference (⚠️):** read-only mode is a setting of the local proxy, so the agent could change it; it is not a control. API tools include `aws___run_script`, which "execute[s] Python code in a sandboxed environment with AWS API access". | ✅ | [Agent Toolkit: getting-started-aws-mcp-server](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/getting-started-aws-mcp-server.html), [understanding-mcp-server-tools](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/understanding-mcp-server-tools.html) |
- How it works: the AWS MCP Server "does not define its own IAM actions". It authenticates the request with the caller's credentials, adds `aws:ViaAWSMCPService` (Boolean, `true` for any request through an AWS managed MCP server) and `aws:CalledViaAWSMCP` (e.g. `aws-mcp.amazonaws.com`, `eks-mcp.amazonaws.com`, `ecs-mcp.amazonaws.com`), and forwards the request. The target service then authorizes it with the caller's own policies.
- Where the keys work: in IAM policies **and SCPs**. Documented examples: "Deny all actions through any AWS managed MCP server", and "Deny destructive actions through AWS MCP Server".
- On direct calls, the IAM condition-keys page says `aws:CalledViaAWSMCP` is "not present when the principal makes the call directly". For `aws:ViaAWSMCPService`, the same page says it "returns `false` when the principal makes the call directly", yet its Availability line says it is included only when an MCP server makes the request. A policy must handle both cases, for example with `BoolIfExists` or `Null` (⚠️ untested).
- OAuth sessions also carry `aws:SignInSessionArn` (2.5.5).

====
| 2.2.5 | **Server-set context keys for agent traffic:**
- How it works: the AWS MCP Server "does not define its own IAM actions". It authenticates the request with the caller's credentials, adds `aws:ViaAWSMCPService` (Boolean, `true` for any request through an AWS managed MCP server) and `aws:CalledViaAWSMCP` (e.g. `aws-mcp.amazonaws.com`, `eks-mcp.amazonaws.com`, `ecs-mcp.amazonaws.com`), and forwards the request. The target service then authorizes it with the caller's own policies.
- Where the keys work: in IAM policies **and SCPs**. Documented examples: "Deny all actions through any AWS managed MCP server", and "Deny destructive actions through AWS MCP Server".
- On direct calls, the IAM condition-keys page says `aws:CalledViaAWSMCP` is "not present when the principal makes the call directly". For `aws:ViaAWSMCPService`, the same page says it "returns `false` when the principal makes the call directly", yet its Availability line says it is included only when an MCP server makes the request. A policy must handle both cases, for example with `BoolIfExists` or `Null` (⚠️ untested).
- OAuth sessions also carry `aws:SignInSessionArn` (2.5.5).

====
| 2.3.4b | **SCP evaluation:**
- "Any account has only those permissions permitted by every parent above it."
- "For a service to be accessible, there must be an explicit allow at every level from the root down to the account."
- "A Deny-only SCP at the root therefore blocks every service unless an explicit Allow covers it."
- So the usual pattern is deny-list SCPs layered on the default `FullAWSAccess` (inference from the limits page: it occupies one of the 10 direct-attachment slots until it is replaced), or explicit allow-lists. A Deny at any level wins.

====
| 2.4.6 | IAM's "revoke active sessions" button does not apply to permission-set roles: "You can't edit roles in IAM that were created from IAM Identity Center permission sets. You must revoke the active permission set session for a user in IAM Identity Center." The page also shows a Deny policy, attached to a role, on `aws:TokenIssueTime` earlier than a chosen time; it revokes that role's sessions issued before then. **Inference (⚠️):** the same condition in an SCP would be an org-wide kill switch. But it would also deny Lambda, ECS and pipeline roles until they refresh their credentials, so it would need careful scoping, for example by `aws:PrincipalArn`. | ✅ / ⚠️ (SCP use) | [IAM id_roles_use_revoke-sessions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_use_revoke-sessions.html) |

====
| 2.5.5 | **AWS MCP Server in CloudTrail:**
- "All AWS MCP Server actions for authenticated tools are logged by CloudTrail". An example is the `CallReadWriteTool` action, whose event includes an "Exact copy of MCP request params" **and** `responseElements.content[].text`, the tool output.
- The sample event has `"eventCategory": "Data"` and `"eventType": "AwsMcpEvent"`. Data events are off by default (2.6.3), and the CloudTrail data-event resource table (read today) has no `aws-mcp` resource type. Yet the MCP page also says the events appear in Event history, which shows only management events (2.6.1). **The docs are inconsistent here. Whether a normal trail records these events, and with which selector, is unverified (⚠️).**
- With OAuth, Sign-In also logs `AuthorizeOAuth2Access` and `CreateOAuth2Token`, including the OAuth client ID and the sign-in session ARN. API calls made with OAuth tokens carry `aws:SignInSessionArn` "to correlate API activity with the originating OAuth sign-in session".
- **PHI note (inference):** request params **and the tool output** are copied into the event, so CloudTrail can hold the data the agent read (1.11, 1.11.4 L15).

====

### 2.9 What this means for Papaya (inferences — to be used in the design)

These are my conclusions from the findings above, not documented facts:

1. **On a laptop, an agent that calls the AWS CLI/SDK directly is indistinguishable from the
   engineer.**
   - **Why:** it uses the same SSO cache, and that cache reaches every role assigned to the
     engineer (2.2.1, 2.2.2). App ID is a client hint (2.2.3). Source identity is trustworthy only
     when the IdP asserts it (2.5.4).
   - **Consequence:** a separate "agent" permission set alone does not separate the two. The
     agent can still use the engineer's other roles from the same cache.
   - **The one native, server-set signal is the AWS MCP Server** (2.2.4, 2.2.5). Calls through it
     carry `aws:ViaAWSMCPService` / `aws:CalledViaAWSMCP`, usable in SCPs. They are absent (or
     false) on direct calls (2.2.5). So the signal is a control only if the agent **cannot make
     direct calls at all**.
   - **Untested design idea, not in the docs (⚠️):** an agent-only role that denies requests not
     made through MCP. AWS documents only the reverse ("deny when via MCP"). The idea helps only if
     the agent cannot reach the engineer's other credentials:
     - **With SigV4,** the local proxy reads the AWS CLI credentials as the same OS user, so this
       needs the proxy outside the agent's sandbox (1.6).
     - **With OAuth,** there are no local AWS credentials, but there is no multi-profile.

     Without that condition, a separate role adds no control. Also to test: whether
     `aws___run_script` and `aws___get_presigned_url` downloads carry the keys. A presigned-URL
     download is made directly by the client.
   - **The decisive layer remains no standing prod-write assignment for humans** (#2). Then
     nothing running on the laptop can write to prod outside an approved, time-boxed window.
     **Inside that window,** any process on the laptop can use the grant. This is a residual risk
     to state openly.
2. **Changing prod: the default path is a pipeline; human write access is the exception, via JIT.**
   - **Default path:** humans hold no prod-write rights. Changes go through CI with a deploy role.
     The named-human approval happens at the CI gate (GitHub Environments, Topic 3).
   - **JIT, for the rest:** when a human needs write access (manual operations, incidents), it
     comes from a JIT assignment. AWS has no native request/approve feature (2.4.1). The options:
     - a partner product (2.4.1);
     - the TEAM sample (2.4.1b);
     - a small home-built flow on `CreateAccountAssignment` / `DeleteAccountAssignment` (2.4.2).
   - **Audit evidence:** CloudTrail records the **grant**, and its caller is the automation role.
     It does **not** record the approver. The approver's identity lives in the approval system
     (GitHub, Linear, the partner tool, TEAM). It must be linked to the grant, for example by
     request ID, and kept as audit evidence (⚠️ design).
   - **Incidents:** under GĐ-8 the incident path is the same flow with a fast approver, not a
     bypass.
   - **Outage path:** the emergency direct-federation path (2.1.11) is for an Identity Center
     outage, and needs its own approval and alerting.
3. **Revocation is slow by design.**
   - Role sessions outlive portal sessions and assignments (2.4.3). IAM's revoke button does not
     apply to permission-set roles (2.4.6).
   - Prod permission sets should use the **1-hour minimum** session duration (2.1.4).
   - Pre-deploy the `identitystore:userId` Deny SCP on the prod OU (2.4.4), and keep the
     `aws:TokenIssueTime` Deny as an org-wide kill switch (2.4.6).
   - Set the portal session length deliberately (2.1.5, 2.1.6), including the IdP session,
     which can silently extend it.
4. **SCPs are the guardrail the agent cannot edit, but only in member accounts.** Examples:
   - protect the org trail and the log archive (2.6.2);
   - deny region drift;
   - deny data-plane reads on PHI buckets and queues, except for the application roles **and**
     the approved JIT read path that GĐ-9 allows (`aws:PrincipalArn`; tenant scoping via ABAC
     session tags, 2.1.8). This supports 1.11.4 L3–L4;
   - deny destructive actions when `aws:ViaAWSMCPService` is true (2.2.5). On its own this is
     bypassed by direct CLI calls (#1), so it is a second layer, not a control.

   Constraints:
   - Keep everything out of the management account (2.3.2, 2.3.7).
   - Deny-list SCPs sit on `FullAWSAccess` (2.3.4b).
   - Limits are 10 direct attachments per target and 10,240 characters each (2.3.4).
   - RCPs add an outside-the-org boundary for S3, SQS, KMS, Secrets Manager and Logs, but not for
     Aurora, Lambda or SNS (2.3.6).
5. **Audit trail for Compliance:**
   - **Trail:** an organization trail to a separate log-archive account, with integrity validation
     and a locked-down bucket (2.6.2, 2.6.4, 2.6.5).
   - **Retention:** decide it explicitly. The default is indefinite, and MFA delete excludes
     lifecycle rules (2.6.5).
   - **Data events:** only where they matter, because of cost (2.6.3): PHI buckets, prod Lambda
     invoke, prod SQS.
   - **No CloudTrail Lake** (2.6.6).
   - **Who did it:** use `onBehalfOf.userId` in CloudTrail where present. Otherwise use the
     session name plus a lookup in the directory (⚠️, 2.5.3). The session name changes when the
     username changes, so it is not a stable key. (`identitystore:UserId` is a policy condition
     key, not a CloudTrail field.)
   - **MCP events:** do not assume AWS MCP Server events are in the trail until the selector
     question is answered (2.5.5).
   - **Aurora:** SQL is invisible to CloudTrail (2.7.1). Use Database Activity Streams or pgaudit,
     alert on the RDS events about lost records, and treat that stream as PHI (2.7.2, 2.7.3).
   - **Same gap for shell sessions:** ECS Exec and SSM shell sessions likely have the same issue
     (⚠️ not researched, 2.10).
6. **Policy changes in Pulumi PRs can be checked mechanically.** `check-no-new-access` in CI makes
   "this PR widens IAM" a visible, reviewable fact (2.8.1; ties to Topics 3–4).

### 2.10 Open items (Topic 2)

- [ ] ⚠️ Does `onBehalfOf.userId` appear on member-account events made with a permission-set role,
      and what exactly is the session name (2.5.3)? Test on a sandbox account.
- [ ] ⚠️ Do profiles sharing one `sso-session` reuse the single cached token (2.2.2)? Test.
- [ ] ⚠️ Agent-only role that denies non-MCP calls (2.9 #1): which condition operator
      (`BoolIfExists` / `Null`), whether `aws___run_script` and presigned-URL downloads carry the
      keys, and whether the proxy can be kept outside the agent's sandbox. Test.
- [ ] ⚠️ Are AWS MCP Server events (`eventCategory: Data`) recorded by a normal trail, and with
      which event selector (2.5.5)?
- [ ] ⚠️ Can permission-set roles (or account-access-manager roles) require `sts:SetSourceIdentity`
      (2.5.4, 2.1.10)?
- [ ] ⚠️ Does Papaya use an external IdP (MFA and session length then live there, 2.1.5, 2.1.7),
      Aurora Serverless v2 (2.7.2), or CloudTrail Lake already (2.6.6)?
- [ ] ⚠️ Not researched: `pgaudit` on Aurora PostgreSQL; Athena over CloudTrail in S3; ECS Exec and
      SSM Session Manager logging of commands; S3 Object Lock for the CloudTrail bucket; whether
      App ID shows in CloudTrail `userAgent`.
